Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00773

Avicenna also says that if the soul changes in one of the outward features, then it would not move the body in the same way. I reply that the earlier thinkers only claimed that whatever moves another thing must itself move in some way. They did not say that both movements must be the same kind. In many cases, the movements caused by the soul are different from the soul’s own movement. The movements of the heavenly bodies are movements of position and depend on the soul’s movement of desire and choice, as Avicenna himself admits. So there is no problem in saying that the soul’s changes in its being or desire cause changes in the body, such as digestion or growth.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00774
Fifth, Avicenna says that the claim that a thing perceives what resembles itself is impossible. We know and perceive many things that are not the sources from which they came.
Book Five: The soul’s inner perceptions
passage-en-00775

I reply that by what is known, I mean the image present to the one who knows it and preserved by that person. The soul is the highest source of the images present in its own powers. It can take in general ideas when it is still only potential intellect; once joined with the active intellect, it creates and preserves them. In his book The Origin and Return, Avicenna says that the potential intellect can strip an image of its material features, then create and receive an intelligible form. It also acts on what is sensed and turns it into something intelligible.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00776
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00777
I. The reasoning soul is not a body and does not have a physical size
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00778

There are several arguments for this. The first begins with our ability to understand general ideas that apply to many different individual things. An idea that applies generally, considered as general, cannot exist inside a body or be imprinted in a bodily part, whether that part is divisible or indivisible.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00779

It cannot exist in an indivisible point. A point cannot contain an intelligible form. Either the point is distinct from the thing whose boundary it marks, or it is not. If it is not distinct, an intelligible form could not be in the point without also being in the body that the point bounds. A point belongs to a magnitude as its boundary. So it could contain only the boundary of something that is already in that magnitude. The form would then be bounded only because the body containing it is bounded. But if the point existed separately from the magnitude, it would itself be divisible—which is impossible, as explained elsewhere.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00780

Someone objects that, even if a point cannot be distinguished from the body it bounds, it does not follow that it can contain only the boundary of something in that body. Colors and light occur on surfaces, not in the depths of a body; the same is true of contact and touching.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00781

The reply is that a surface can be considered in two ways: as the boundary of a body, or as a two-dimensional, extended part of it. Colors and light belong to it as an extended part, not simply as a boundary. For something to receive a quality, it must have a particular readiness or condition that enables it to receive that quality. A boundary, just as a boundary, has no varying power or readiness. So if a point could receive an intelligible form, it would always receive one: nothing in it could change to make it ready at one time and not another. The form would always be present, since the source of its flow gives it continuously.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00782

And if the point were ready by its very nature, every body containing a point would be able to understand. Anyone dying would also remain able to understand, since the point that made this possible would still be there. That conclusion is false, so the claim that a point can receive an intelligible form must also be false.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00783

Nor can an idea understood by the mind be contained in a divisible part of a body. Every magnitude can be divided, and anything present in a divisible thing must itself be divisible. So the intelligible form would have to be divided without end. This is impossible for several reasons.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00784

First, the parts would have to be either alike or different. They cannot be alike. Each part would have to differ from the whole in some way, since a part cannot be equal to the whole in every respect. The difference cannot be in the form’s essential nature or in what necessarily follows from that nature; otherwise, the parts would not be alike. So it would have to come from material features such as size or shape. The form would then be material, which contradicts the claim that it is immaterial.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00785

Second, suppose the form’s being understood depended on its division. Then the parts would have to differ from the whole, and before the division the form would not be understood, since the required condition was absent. Anything understood in this way would have to be divisible, though many things we understand are not. If division is not a condition for understanding, then dividing the form would merely cover it with accidental features, such as being gathered or separated. A smaller part of the body would then be enough to contain the form’s nature, because a part of the form has the same nature as the whole. Its place would be only a part of the body’s place. The entire form could therefore be present in a smaller part of its supposed location. Its presence there would be accidental, not essential. But we are discussing an immaterial form, so this is impossible.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00786

You might object that an idea understood by the mind can be divided into similar parts by adding further universal features. Take the general idea “animal.” It can be divided into the animal nature found in a human being and the animal nature found in a horse. These two animal natures are alike in kind: if we leave out the horse’s neighing and the human being’s rationality, their animal nature is the same. So a universal can apparently be divided into similar parts, even though those parts have no particular size or shape.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00787

I reply that this is a different kind of division. Adding one universal idea to another is combination, while dividing a whole into parts is separation. For example, adding “rational” to “animal” makes the human kind different from the horse kind. But dividing a whole into parts makes the parts equal to the whole in nature. If the parts of an intelligible form were like its separate instances, then the universal form would have to differ from every one of its parts. Its division would not be a division of magnitude, though we assumed that it was. In short, dividing “animal” into human being, horse, and other kinds divides a universal into its particular forms by adding different limits to it. The proposed division of an intelligible form is a division of a whole into parts. The two are clearly different.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00788

Nor can the form be divided into parts with different meanings. If it were, those parts would have to be its kinds and distinguishing features. But the parts we can imagine in a body have no limit in number. That would mean that the intelligible form had infinitely many essential parts, which is impossible.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00789

There are further reasons. In any multitude there must be a definite number of units. If the form had infinitely many parts, each part would have to be a simple nature and therefore could not itself be divided into two parts with different natures. Also, if the form were made of infinitely many essential parts, each present in a different bodily part, the body itself would have infinitely many actual parts. That is impossible. Finally, suppose we divide the form so that its distinguishing feature lies on one side and its general kind on the other. If we make a different division, either each side contains half of both the feature and the kind—giving two similar parts, already shown to be impossible—or the kind and feature move into the new parts. Then simply imagining a different division would move the parts of the form from one place to another. Their location would depend on what someone chose to imagine, which is absurd.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00790

A second argument against dividing an intelligible form begins from the nature of a thing. Every thing has a reality by which it is what it is. That reality must be one, and cannot itself be divided. For something that can be divided must remain through the division. But ten, considered precisely as ten, does not remain when divided: five is not part of ten considered as a kind of number. It is part of the many units that make up ten, not part of ten considered as one reality. When ten is divided into two fives, they are parts of ten as a multitude, not of ten as one. Its multiplicity is measured by what is counted, not by ten itself: ten people are many in relation to one person, but ten is one number. It therefore has one form that cannot be divided.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00791

If knowledge of these immaterial realities were present in a divisible place, then dividing that place would divide the knowledge, and dividing the knowledge would divide what it represents. But what is known is not divided, or is understood precisely as undivided. That is impossible.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00792

This is how the argument is usually presented in the books of the philosophers. They consider it one of the strongest proofs that the human souls which understand universal meanings are immaterial. But, as I have said, not every human soul has full intellectual immateriality. In my view, this argument does not apply to every soul. It proves the immateriality of a soul that understands a form as actually intelligible in itself, whether because the form’s nature is immaterial or because the mind has abstracted it from what the senses perceive. Such a soul has moved beyond intellect as a mere capacity and become an intellect in reality, with ideas actually understood. Only some people reach this level.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00793

Most people’s understanding of universal kinds works more like the way natural kinds exist in the world through their particular instances. Consider “animal” as animal. Its nature exists in the world through individual animals. We can consider that nature without limiting it to one place or position, but its shared nature can also be divided into particular instances. In the minds of most people, the nature of an animal exists through an imagined image. The mind can consider this image in different ways. As a particular image in a particular perceptive power, it is an imagined particular. Considered simply as what it is—animal, with no added condition—it is neither imagined, sensed, nor understood, because in that respect its existence is indeterminate, though it exists in reality through the image. Considered as common to many things, it is understood as an immaterial universal.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00794

So what exists in most people’s minds is not an immaterial form whose own existence is like that of separate intellects. It is something that can be considered in different ways: as particular, as universal, or without either qualification. The same is true of the form of that nature in the world outside the mind. Nor do I agree that everyone can notice these different ways of considering it, or that everyone can grasp a mental form precisely as universal and shared by many, free of all particular limits.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00795

I also question the second argument’s claim that every thing’s unity is wholly opposed to division, so that its form must be indivisible too. Many things are one while also being divisible, either actually, as a number is, or potentially, as a body or magnitude is. Ten is one number, but its unity is also the many units that compose it. That many is not the multiplicity opposed to ten. The multiplicity opposed to the unity of ten is a set of tens; the unity of ten is itself the many tenths. Likewise, the unity of five is the many fifths. As we have seen, number has a weak kind of existence because its unity is also a multitude.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00796

The same is true of bodies, magnitudes, and other continuous things. Their unity is their ability to be divided, in thought or in reality, because their unity consists in being continuous and extended. Extension means that they can be divided into parts, either potentially or actually. We therefore cannot find in such things a kind of unity that has no relation to multiplicity at all. Their unity differs from the kind of multiplicity that opposes it, but not from the multiplicity already contained within it. Many scholars, including Avicenna in The Healing, have missed this point. To show that unity differs from existence, he says that a multitude is something that exists, but a multitude as multitude is not one. The problem with this argument has already been explained.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00797

The philosophers also offer another version of this argument. They consider things that cannot be divided by reason, such as God, unity, and the simple realities that make up complex things. If a complex reality exists, it must ultimately contain simple realities, since every multitude includes unity. They then ask: if knowledge of such a simple reality is divided, are its parts each pieces of knowledge or not? If they are not, then knowledge is not the sum of those parts; it is the whole formed when they come together. The question then concerns that whole: if it were divided, would its parts be knowledge? If so, each part must be about something. Is each part about the whole thing known, or about only a part of it? If each part were about the whole, a part of knowledge would equal the whole in every respect, which is impossible. If it were about a part, then the simple reality known would have parts, though we have shown that it has none. They say this is the best form of the argument.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00798

I reply that not every human soul can imagine the true nature of these simple realities. When most people try to understand them, they picture imaginary shapes or forms with size. How could they know the Creator in His essence or simple intellectual realities? The argument is soundest when applied to souls that know God and separate forms as they truly are. Very few souls reach that level. Other souls are free of natural bodies but not of imagined forms.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00799

Some later thinkers object that a point must either exist in a divisible part of a body, in which case an indivisible thing would be in something divisible, or in an indivisible part, which would mean there are indivisible particles. They also object that unity, though far removed from multiplicity, is present in bodies; that fatherhood is present in a father though it cannot be divided; and that estimation is a bodily power even though the hostility it perceives cannot be divided into halves or quarters. The same, they say, is true of friendship and similar meanings.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00800

The first objection is answered by recognizing that a point does not belong to a body considered simply as a divisible thing. It belongs to the body insofar as its extension has an end or is cut off. The body contains a point as its boundary, and a boundary involves an absence: it is where extension runs out. This differs from knowledge, which completes the thing that has it.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00801

As for unity, I have explained that the unity of a body is divisible because it is the body’s continuity and extension. Its existence is also its being a body. It is remarkable that the unity of a body is divided directly when the body itself is divided, not indirectly as other features are divided when their subject is divided. Blackness, for example, is divided only because the body that has it is divided. The unity of a body is its very existence and individual identity.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00802

As for fatherhood and other relations, I do not agree that every relation is divided along with its subject. Relations that belong to a body just as a body—being alongside or touching another thing, for example—are divided with it. Half a body alongside something is half the relation of the whole body; a quarter of the body is a quarter of that relation. But some relations belong to a body because of something other than its bodily nature. These need not be divided when the body is divided. Zayd’s fatherhood, for example, does not belong to him because of his size or his being a body, but because of another feature, such as a soul’s power to generate. The last objection is answered by what I said earlier: estimation is immaterial, though it remains connected to matter, and the same is true of what it perceives.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00803

The second proof is one Avicenna relied on in his Discussions. I believe it is his strongest argument on this subject. His students raised many objections, and he answered them. I found their questions and replies scattered through a collection of letters between him and his students. I will present them here in order, with some additions of my own.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00804

We can understand ourselves. Whoever understands a thing has its reality present to them. So the reality of our own self is present to us. Either we understand ourselves because another image, equal to our self, has appeared in us, or because our self itself is present to us. The first is impossible: it would mean that two identical things came together. So the second must be true. Whatever has itself present to itself exists in itself. The soul, then, is a substance that exists in itself. Every body or bodily thing depends on something else to exist; therefore the soul is not bodily.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00805

The questioner says: I do not accept that being aware of ourselves means that the true reality of our self is present to us. Perhaps some effect of the self appears in us, and we become aware of that effect. It would not be the self itself. In that case, the reality of the self produces an effect in us, and we notice the effect; it is not the self that appears in us twice.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00806

The respondent says: We have already established that awareness means that the reality of a thing is present. If you say that an effect of the self appears in us and we become aware of that effect, either awareness is that same effect, or it is something different that follows from it. If awareness is the effect itself, then saying that we become aware of the effect adds nothing to saying that the effect appears in us. If awareness follows the effect, then either awareness is the presence of the thing’s own reality or the presence of some other reality. If it is some other reality, then awareness would mean that something other than the thing’s reality gives us the thing’s meaning. If it is the thing’s own reality, then the self’s reality would need this effect in order to be present to itself. It would not exist until the effect brought it into being. It would then be created by the effect, not affected by it, which is absurd. Or perhaps you mean that the self’s reality is present to us in another way, by being stripped of some features or newly formed. Then what we understand is that changed or stripped-down form. But our question concerns the enduring substance of the self, which is understood as the same in both cases.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00807

The questioner says: Let us agree that we understand ourselves. Why say that whoever understands a thing has the reality of that thing present? If that were so, when we understood God and the active intellects, their true realities would have to be present in us.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00808

The respondent says: What we receive from the active intellect, if we can understand it, is its kind and nature, not its individual self. The two are not the same in every respect. But what we understand of your reality does not differ from your reality in kind, in nature, or in any added feature; nor does it differ from you as an individual. It is you yourself in kind and as an individual. The active intellect and what we understand of it are the same in meaning, but not the same individual.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00809

I reply that the specific nature of the active intellect cannot have multiple individuals, either in the world or in the mind. Proof shows that each separate intellect is the only individual of its kind. If one nature had multiple individuals, each would have to be distinguished by some feature that was not essential to the kind. But an accidental feature would require an external cause and a subject capable of change. The intellect would then not be separate from matter, which is impossible. The better answer is that what appears in our minds of these simple realities is not their innermost nature. We know only general ideas such as “separate substance,” “intellect,” and the like.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00810
The questioner says: If an image equal to God’s nature appears in our intellect, then God’s nature must apply to many things in the world.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00811
The respondent says: Proof shows only that God’s nature does not apply to many things in the world; it does not show that it cannot apply to many things in the mind.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00812

I reply: God’s reality cannot be a nature that could be shared by many, either in the world or in the mind. He is pure, self-subsisting existence, complete beyond anything else. Anything with a general nature has an identity beyond that nature. Existence itself is individual identity. So anything that has a nature or essence is only possibly existent. The right answer is that we do not know the Creator’s essence itself. We know Him through features that point to Him, or by saying what He is not.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00813

The questioner says: Let us agree that when we understand something, its nature is present to us. Why can’t the self be present in our power of estimation, which then becomes aware of it—just as the intellect is aware of estimation? The intellect would then not be present to itself, only to estimation, just as you say that estimation is not present to itself but to the intellect.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00814

The respondent says: Your awareness of your own identity is not the work of one of your powers. Otherwise, the one aware of your self would not be the self you are aware of. Yet when you are aware of yourself, you know that you yourself are both the one who is aware and the one you are aware of. If another power were aware of your self, either that power would exist in you, or it would not. If it existed in you, then your enduring self would be present to that power, and so would be present to itself—which is what we wanted to show. If the power were not in you but in a body, then either your self would exist in that body or it would not. If it did not, there would be no awareness of your self at all, only a body sensing something other than itself, as your hand or foot senses something. If your self did exist in that body, then both the self and the power aware of it would exist in something else. The self could not be aware of itself through that power, since both the self and the power would belong to that body.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00815
The questioner asks: Could I be aware of myself because an image of me appears in something whose relation to me is like a mirror’s relation to sight?
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00816

The respondent says: Even if we agree that your image appears in the mirror, it must then appear a second time in the eye. In the same way, the image of the self would have to appear in the self again.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00817

The questioner asks: Could awareness of myself come from another image appearing in me? When I understand Zayd’s soul, either I am not aware of myself at that time—which is impossible, since anyone who understands something is also potentially aware of themselves—or I am aware of myself too. In that case, either two images are present, one of me and one of Zayd, or there is only one. If there is one image, then I would be Zayd and Zayd would be me: the same image would have my features in one respect and Zayd’s in another. If there are two images, that proves my point.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00818

The respondent says: When you understand a soul, you understand one part of your own reality. When you understand that Zayd is human, you add something else to your self and join it to what you already know. The idea “humanity” does not appear twice in you; it is one idea considered in two ways. Keep in mind that there is a difference between humanity considered in itself and humanity considered as universal and shared by many. The first is an essential part; the second is humanity with the added condition of being universal.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00819

The questioner says: The distinction you have made is false. If we say that a thing exists in itself, this can mean three things. First, it does not depend on anything else in order to exist. Second, it is not present in something else, as whiteness is present in a body. Both meanings are negative, while awareness is something positive: it means that the known form is present to the knower. Third, it could mean that the thing is related to itself. But that is impossible, since a relation requires two things and unity rules this out. You cannot reply that the one who relates and the thing related may be either the same or different. That is a verbal trick. “A cause requires an effect” can also mean that the cause and effect are either the same or different, but that does not prove that a thing can cause itself. The same applies here.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00820

The respondent says: A thing’s true reality is one thing; its individual identity is another. The underlying whole is one, while its individual identity is something else. This is true whether that identity necessarily belongs to its nature, as with God and the active intellects, or whether it does not, as with kinds that have many individual members. That degree of difference is enough for a relation to be valid. It is therefore right to say “my self” and “your self.”
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00821

I reply that this answer is weak. In a truly simple being, whose identity is its very own, there are not two distinct aspects, a reality and an identity. I have already answered this problem about a simple being’s knowledge of itself, in the discussion of relations and of knowledge.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00822

The questioner objects that animals perceive themselves, even though their souls are not immaterial. We should not accept the claim that they are unaware of themselves. They seek what suits them and flee what harms them. Their goal cannot be simply whatever suits them in general; otherwise, they would seek what suits other animals as eagerly as what suits themselves. Nor can they seek what suits them specifically because it is suitable in general: that would require them to understand a universal, which animals do not. So an animal seeks what suits itself in particular, and to do so it must perceive itself. Knowing that one thing is related to another requires knowing both things.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00823

The respondent says: The human soul is aware of itself directly, but other animal souls are aware of themselves through their power of estimation, using the organ of estimation, just as they perceive other things through the senses and their organs. In animals, estimation perceives particular meanings that cannot be sensed but are linked to what is sensed. That is how animals perceive their own selves. They do not perceive themselves through their essence or through the heart, which is the organ of their essence, but through estimation and its organ. So an animal’s self is present once in the organ of its own life—the heart—and again in the organ of estimation, where it is perceived as present.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00824
The questioner asks: What proves that our awareness of ourselves differs from an animal’s?
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00825

The respondent says: The power that understands universal ideas can understand its own nature stripped of all accidental features. When we are aware of our particular self, mixed with other things, we are aware of a whole made of parts that we can recognize separately: our own true self and the things mixed with it. The self can be represented to us even when everything else is absent. An animal’s awareness of itself is not like this. That shows the difference.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00826

I reply that this is really a retreat from the second proof to the first. The truth is that animals are aware of themselves through their own awareness, by an imagined rather than intellectual awareness. This does not depend on an organ of imagination. It shows that they are separate from natural bodies, though not from imagined forms. I have already proved that the imaginative souls of this world are immaterial. The difference between them and the highest human souls is that the latter can perceive themselves free of all distances, images, shapes, and the like.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00827

The questioner says: Even if we can distinguish ourselves in the mind from what is mixed with us, it does not follow that this distinction exists outside the mind. We make this distinction by thought, while reality may be different. This applies whether we perceive ourselves as universal or as particular and mixed with other things. In truth, anything that perceives something has that thing present to it, whether universal or particular. When a donkey perceives its own mixed-up self, its self is present to it. So in every case, the donkey’s self exists for it. That can only be through one power, which means the self is immaterial.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00828

The argument that a power other than the donkey’s self perceives it also fails. If the perceiver is not the self but another power, that power is either in the donkey or elsewhere. If it is in the donkey, then the donkey’s self is present in the donkey. If it is elsewhere, then the perceiver is not what it perceives, and the donkey does not perceive itself—something already disproved. Even if we agree that the donkey perceives itself through one of its parts, that part must contain an image of the donkey’s self, and so that part too would be immaterial. Also, if the donkey’s self were present in the organ of its power of estimation, though mixed with other things, that organ should be alive through the donkey’s self just as the organ of the self is alive through it. Some reply that the image in estimation is like the green color that appears by reflection, while its presence in its own organ is like the original green color. This is all that has been said on the question; the fuller answer is the one I have already indicated.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00829

The third argument is closely related to the first. Our souls can understand the universal idea “human being,” which is shared by all human individuals. The idea must be free of any one position or shape, or it could not be shared by people with different positions and shapes. This universal form clearly exists. Since universals do not exist outside the mind, it must exist in the mind. Its home must either be a body or something nonbodily. It cannot be a body, since it would then have a particular size and position through its bodily subject, and would no longer be universal. So the place where this form exists is not a body. It is a being whose existence does not depend on matter.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00830

Someone may ask: Does the universal intelligible form of a human being exist? If it does not, how can we say that it must have a certain kind of home? If it does, then surely it is a particular image in the particular human soul. Universals cannot exist as such in the outside world. As a particular image in one person’s soul, it is not shared by many people. First, what is particular cannot be shared. Second, the image is an accident in the soul, while individual human beings are substances that exist in themselves. How can the reality of a substance be an accident that exists in something else?
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00831

They may answer that a form is universal because whichever human being first acts on the soul, the same kind of effect would appear in it. If a horse had been the first thing to act on the soul, a different effect would have appeared.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00832

But then why could such an image not exist in a bodily place? Suppose seeing one particular human being creates an image in the brain that would be the same no matter which human being was first seen. They might reply that, if the image existed in the body, it would have a particular size and shape because of the body, which would prevent it from being universal.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00833

But the image in an individual soul is also particular and an accident in a particular subject. That too should prevent it from being universal. If the size and shape an image gains by existing in a body prevent it from being universal, then the individual unity and status as an accident that it gains by existing in a particular soul should also prevent it. If, however, the image in the soul can be considered in another way and so count as universal, then an image in the brain or another bodily matter could also be considered in another way and count as universal, even though it is particular in size, shape, and position. In short, whether a form exists in the soul or in the body, it is not shared in every respect, because its individual unity prevents that. Yet in another respect it can still be shared.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00834

I reply that this is a difficult objection, raised in discussions of knowledge and universals. We have answered it by saying that what makes a form universal and shareable is its intellectual mode of existence. A form can be one particular thing with its own identity and still, through its intellectual existence, apply equally to many. An intellectual identity does not prevent universality. What prevents sharing is material existence: a bodily individual has a specific position, place, and size, so its relation to other bodily individuals differs. We do not need to posit one way of considering the form as universal and another way of considering it as an individual thing. Its intellectual existence is itself a different, fuller kind of existence, not confined to one particular instance. Natures and meanings can be applied to many things, and this remains true when they exist intellectually without any particular position or size.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00835

You already know from our account of intellect and intelligible forms that understanding is not a matter of an intelligible image settling into the intellect as an accident in a substance. The intellectual forms of substances are themselves substances, existing in themselves and through their source. In being and in their way of existing as substances, they are stronger than the material forms they represent, which depend on matter that keeps changing and being changed. But does this argument truly prove that souls are immaterial?
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00836

I say that the argument is decisive, but it proves that some human souls do not depend on matter, not that this is true of ordinary people in general. It applies to a soul that understands things without relying on bodily images and apprehends them in the way intellect knows them, a mode shared by many individual instances. This is possible only after one meaning has been stripped of its limits, additions, and particular features. In short, it applies to anyone who can consider, for example, the form of an animal in a way that gives it no particular size, place, position, or time.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00837

The same is true of understanding the purely intellectual form of a human being. We must think of a human being with all features that are not humanity itself removed, such as a particular place, size, and position, while keeping all the parts and powers that belong to a human being. We must understand it as having a head, face, eyes, hands, feet, and belly, all in a way that is intellectual and shared by many individuals. This is what it means to understand a universal nature. As the First Teacher says in the Theology of Aristotle, the intellectual human being is spiritual, and all its parts are spiritual. The eye’s place is not separate from the hand’s place, and the bodily parts do not occupy different locations. In the same way, we can understand intellectual earth, water, or heaven, and hold in mind the form of any nature in its intellectual mode, as explained above. This is what it means to understand universals. Few people can understand in this way. Most people imagine, for example, a human image in their imagination. When they sense another individual, they notice that this one is like the first and imagine the common feature between them. This is an imaginative understanding, like sensing that all the different portions of water are water, or that separate drops are all water.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00838

The fourth argument is that the intellect can perform an unlimited number of acts, while no bodily power can do so. Therefore, no intellectual power is bodily. The first claim is clear: we can understand numbers, and their sequence has no end. This is one kind of thing the intellect understands. The proof of the second claim was given earlier. The author of the Discussions says that to prove bodily powers are limited in their activity, we must show that they are divided along with their bodily subject. That brings back the objections to the first argument: the point, unity, relations, and the particular meanings perceived by estimation.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00839

I have already answered these objections, praise be to God. The writer of The Discussions then raises further questions about this argument. First, we do not accept that the rational power can understand infinitely many things all at once. It can keep understanding more, without reaching a final limit, but that does not mean it can perform infinitely many acts. A body too can be divided again and again without reaching a final limit, but it cannot actually undergo infinitely many divisions. The same may be true of the intellect: it may be capable of an unending sequence of acts without being capable of infinitely many acts at once.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00840

Second, even if the intellect can deal with infinitely many things, why call this an unlimited number of acts? Understanding is a kind of being affected, not an act. You allow that bodily things can be affected an unlimited number of times. Your own theory says that prime matter has received an unlimited number of forms over time.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00841
Third, this argument seems to fail for the souls of the heavenly spheres. You say these souls depend on bodies, yet their act—circular motion—continues without end.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00842

The reply to the first question is that the rational power plainly does not reach a final limit beyond which it could no longer understand more. We have also proved that bodily powers cannot be like this. That is enough for the argument.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00843

Someone may object: A bodily power might continue to exist forever. Either it must reach a time when it can no longer exist and becomes impossible, or it never reaches such a point. The first option is false, since what is possible in itself cannot become impossible in itself. So perhaps a bodily power can always continue to exist and act. If so, it might have unlimited effects, which would undermine the argument.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00844

I reply that possibility and impossibility in themselves are features of a nature considered in relation to existence. Powers, however, are existing, individual things, and their particular existence includes a particular time. A certain kind of existence may be necessary, while another kind is impossible, without changing the possibility of the shared nature considered in itself. The proof concerns one individual bodily thing performing unlimited acts, not a kind of thing that has many individuals. Numerical unity is not the same as unity of kind.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00845
As for the second question, even if understanding itself is being affected, the soul acts when it arranges and analyzes its premises. That is enough for our argument.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00846

I reply that a power’s ability to be affected cannot be separated from its ability to act, even though these are different aspects. A thing must exist before it can be affected by something else. A bodily power cannot perform unlimited acts, and so it cannot undergo unlimited effects either. The objection from prime matter fails because prime matter does not remain as one enduring individual. Its unity is weak and indeterminate; as it takes on different forms, it changes and is renewed, as explained earlier.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00847

You might ask: Haven’t you distinguished the common sense, which perceives, from the imaginative power, which rearranges what it perceives? A single power cannot both perceive and rearrange. How, then, can you say that the soul acts by arranging and joining premises and is affected by receiving images?
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00848
I reply that the soul has two powers, a practical one and a knowing one. It acts through one and receives through the other.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00849

As for the third objection, some say the souls of the heavenly spheres depend on bodies but do not act independently. Their power is limited in themselves but becomes unlimited through the light of intellect that reaches them. An objection follows: if the intellect gives the sphere a moving power, then that power is bodily, and we have a bodily source of unlimited action. If the intellect itself produces the movement, then the bodily power is not its source, and the movement would not truly be the sphere’s own. This also seems to make a body receptive to the separate intellect’s influence without any bodily power, which is impossible.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00850

I reply that this objection would hold only if the intellect’s influence passed through one numerically identical power or one fixed addition to the sphere. But the separate intellect may continuously give the sphere new powers, or new qualities that keep changing. Neither problem would then follow. We have already discussed something similar.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00851

Still, if this is possible for the bodily powers of the spheres, why could the rational power not also be bodily, yet capable of unlimited acts through the light it receives from the active intellect? The imaginative power seems to support this concern: although it is not intellect, it can form an unlimited number of images because it draws from the intellectual world.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00852

The fifth argument is this. If the intellect were imprinted in a body, such as the heart or brain, it would either always understand that body or never understand it. The conclusion is false, so the intellect is not imprinted in a body. The reasoning is that it understands the body either because the body’s own outward form is present to the intellect, or because another image of that bodily organ appears in the intellect. If the first, the intellect would always understand that organ. If the second, two matching images would have to exist in the same place: the image of the organ that understands and the image of the organ being understood. Then understanding would be impossible. Also, there is no reason why one of the two images should be the perceiver and the other the perceived.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00853

Someone might say that the second image exists in the first image, not in its bodily matter. That would make the first image the perceiver and the second the thing perceived. I reply that we would again have to explain why one image is the home of the other and not the other way around. So if understanding the body requires another image of it, the intellect cannot understand that body.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00854

The conclusion that the intellect either always or never understands the body is also false, since sometimes we understand a bodily organ and sometimes we do not. The argument is a conditional proof: if the intellect were in a body, then it would either always understand that body or never understand it; but in fact it sometimes understands it and sometimes does not. So it is not in a body. To establish this, we need four points. First, to understand a thing, its form must be present to whoever understands it. Second, if something perceives through itself, the form must be present in it. If it perceives through an organ, the form must be present in that organ. Third, bodily things act through the bodies in which they exist. Those bodies serve as their tools. Fourth, things of the same kind differ only through features of their matter.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00855

I reply that we do not accept the second point. You know that sight perceives visible things without their forms being imprinted in the eye, and imagination perceives bodily images without their being imprinted in the brain. This argument therefore fails because one of its premises is unsound.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00856

The author of the Discussions challenges the first point. He has often said that knowing something does not require the thing’s form to be present to the knower. Knowledge is a relation that may occur with or without the form being present. In every case, he says, knowledge is this particular relation. Why could the rational soul not exist in a body, with knowledge arising whenever this relation exists between the soul and the body?
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00857

I have already shown that knowledge cannot be a bare relation. A relation can exist only when something exists that the relation connects. We have explained how a relation depends on its terms and is not an independent thing.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00858

The author also replies that the thing we understand as “heaven” is not equal in nature to the actual heaven. If it were, then black would be the same in nature as white. Black and white have more in common—both are qualities in a body we can sense—than the intelligible form of heaven has with the actual heaven, which is a substance we can sense and that surrounds the earth.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00859

The reply is that what we understand by “heaven” is the nature that makes heaven what it is, present in an immaterial mode of existence, without bodily position or direction. If the claim is that the intelligible heaven differs from the perceptible heaven because one is understood and the other sensed, that is true. If the claim is that what we understand is not the nature of heaven, it is false. And if the claim is that one is a substance and the other an accident, that too is false, as explained above.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00860

Al-Tusi, in his commentary on Pointers, accepts that the intelligible heaven is an accident in an immaterial subject. He distinguishes its relation to the perceptible heaven from the relation between blackness and whiteness. The first difference is between one nature understood with its features and the same nature considered alongside their opposites. The difference between black and white, by contrast, is between two species formed by opposite distinguishing features.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00861

I reply that stripping away accompanying features is not required in order to understand a nature. The intellect can understand a human being with all their features—size, quality, place, position, clothing, shape, and body parts—but in a universal, intellectual way. This is established in the discussion of God’s knowledge of particular things. To understand something intellectually, we must strip away its bodily mode of existence and consider it in an intellectual mode. The difference between the understood heaven and the sensed heaven lies only in their modes of existence. Whatever exists in the one true, luminous mode, which cannot be hidden, multiplied, or divided, is intelligible in itself. Whatever exists in this bodily, material mode is hidden even from itself, let alone from anything else. It knows itself only through a faint light it receives from the higher existence.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00862

Another objection is that if the intellect contains an image equal to the body it understands, there is no problem of two matching forms in one place: one form exists in the intellect, while the other exists in the intellect’s bodily subject.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00863

The reply, as given in the commentary on Pointers, is that if the intellectual power could contain a form without that form being present in its bodily subject, then a bodily power would act without the body’s participation. But every bodily agent acts with the body’s participation. Anything that acts without such participation is not bodily. The intellect would then be nonbodily, which is the very point at issue. If the form were present in the subject as well, the original problem of two matching forms would return. Someone may say that the difference is clear: one form exists in the intellect and its subject, while the other exists only in the subject. I reply that this kind of “presence” is just a pairing of two things. It makes no sense to pair a form with one of two closely connected things and not with the other. In any case, the problem of two forms of the same kind in one place remains.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00864
The same argument would also seem to show that the soul either always understands its own qualities and features or never understands any of them.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00865

It would also seem to show that it always knows all its changing features, so long as they are present. Otherwise, it would need another image of each feature in order to know it, and two matching forms would be present in one place.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00866

Al-Tusi replies that the soul’s features fall into two groups. Some belong to it by its very nature, such as being aware of itself. Others belong to it when compared with things different from itself, such as not depending on matter and not belonging to another thing as one of its properties. The soul is always aware of the first group, just as it is always aware of itself. It is aware of the second only when the conditions are present.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00867

I reply that this does not answer the second version of the objection. We can answer it by saying that the soul’s features are its knowledge and acts of awareness, together with what follows from them. Whenever these kinds of knowledge are present, the soul is aware of them through the very forms that are present. When the soul is unaware of them, they are no longer present. The same applies to feelings such as anger, desire, embarrassment, and fear, which involve the body.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00868

The sixth argument is that if the intellect were bodily, it would always weaken in old age. But it does not always weaken then. So the intellect is not bodily. We can express this as a proof: the power by which an older person understands is an intellect, and not every power by which an older person understands grows weak with age. Therefore, not every intellect grows weak with age. It is enough for this argument if even one person’s intellect does not weaken; we need not claim that no older person ever loses intellectual power.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00869

The argument does not say that an older person’s understanding is never affected when the body is ill or weak. That would merely show that bodily powers can interfere with understanding. A bodily power may be needed at first to prepare something for the intellect to understand. Or the soul’s attention to the body may distract it from other acts. This is like a traveler with a poor horse: having to look after the horse may keep the traveler from other tasks, though the tasks themselves are not performed by the horse. Likewise, an older person may turn from intellectual activity to caring for the body, or a bodily organ may be impaired and needed at the beginning of intellectual activity because the soul is still weak and its understanding not yet established.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00870

If someone says that an older person can keep thinking clearly because the intellect uses a bodily organ that decays later than the others, the reply is that the outer organs weaken because the inner organs have already begun to fail. If those inner organs remained healthy, the outer ones would keep their power. But an older person’s liver, brain, and heart are not in their healthy state, or anything close to it. We can see this from changes in the pulse, urine, and brain activity. And the intellect does not need the hands, feet, or skin in order to complete its work.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00871

I reply that the changes that come with old age also follow changes in the soul. As you know, the soul is what first shapes the body and its balance. The body and its powers grow weak because the soul turns, by its nature, from caring for this life toward caring for another. This is the wisdom behind natural death, not the cause given by doctors and others.
Book Six: How the reasoning soul exists without depending on matter, and how it begins to exist
passage-en-00872

If you say that perhaps an older person’s bodily balance is better suited to intellectual activity and this is why their intellect is stronger, I reply: no. An older person’s body is either cold and dry or weak and frail. Both conditions occur in people who are not old, and they do not give them greater intellectual ability. Weakness of the body may well suit what does not depend on the body. This is a divinely inspired insight.
